title: Knowledge starts with humility
hook: Arjuna argues like an expert, then says: teach me. The Gita's list of knowledge starts there.
tomorrow: The same Lord in all beings

segments.voice: Yesterday, kshetra: the body is the field; you're its knower. Today, what the knower actually knows.
screen: `KSHETRA: THE BODY IS THE FIELD; YOU'RE ITS KNOWER.`

segments.voice: At the start of the Gita, Arjuna argues like an expert. He's a great archer and a prince, and he lays out the case against this war: family will be destroyed, the old ways will fall, it's wrong to kill your own teachers. Then, a few verses into chapter two, he stops. He admits his mind is confused about what's right. And he says to Krishna: I am your student. I've taken refuge in you. Teach me. That's the moment the Gita really begins. Not when Arjuna knows the most, but when he admits he doesn't.
screen: `ARJUNA ARGUES LIKE AN EXPERT.` → `THEN: I AM YOUR STUDENT.` → `TEACH ME.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen turns that moment into a list. Verse seven. Krishna gives a heading, knowledge, and the first word under it is amanitva: humility, not thinking much of yourself. Then adambhitva, no pretending. Then ahimsa, doing no harm. Then patience, straightforwardness, serving your teacher, cleanliness, steadiness, self-control. In many Hindu homes that line still lives in the body: you bow, or touch an elder's feet, before you learn from them. The list keeps going. Not being dragged by the senses. Not being ruled by the sense of I. Not clinging too tightly to home and family. Staying even when things go well and when they don't. Steady devotion. A taste for quiet places. Then the surprise. This, Krishna says, is called knowledge, and whatever is its opposite is ajnana, ignorance. So in the Gita, knowledge isn't only what's in your head; it's how you live. A brilliant, arrogant person, by this definition, is missing the first item. From verse twelve the chapter turns to what is to be known, Brahman, and the words go strange on purpose. It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes and faces everywhere. It's far away, and it's near, inside beings and outside them. Verse seventeen calls it the light of lights, beyond darkness. And the door to it starts where Arjuna started: humility.
screen: `FIRST ON THE LIST: HUMILITY.` · `BOW BEFORE YOU LEARN.` · `THE OPPOSITE IS IGNORANCE.` · `KNOWLEDGE IS HOW YOU LIVE.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE STARTS WITH HUMILITY.`

segments.voice: Think of a recent moment you needed to be right, a text thread, a meeting, a family dinner, and just see it. Replay it with the need dropped one notch: ask a question instead of making a point. Then do what Arjuna did. If you pray, bow your head and ask God, teach me. If you don't, say it inwardly to the day ahead: i don't know everything yet. Notice how that softer version feels in the chest.
Amanitva, humility, not thinking much of yourself. Gita thirteen, seven: the first word on the list Krishna calls knowledge; its opposite is ignorance.
Your line: amanitva: knowledge begins with humility. Arjuna's did: teach me. Day two hundred five, done.

screen: `DAY 205 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SAME LORD IN ALL BEINGS.`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote Gita 13.7–13.11 as a checklist of character for students, starting with amanitva, humility; many traditions treat serving and honoring the teacher as part of this knowledge.

original.note: Sanskrit: amanitva, humility, literally not-being-proud; the first item in Gita 13's list of knowledge.
